I think I like this overall. Documentation is important here. Also I'd like to keep the `extraConfig` escape hatch.

One (admittedly minor) drawback is that it can feel a little bit uncanny-valley like when the upstream configuration options don't adhere to nix conventions like starting with a lowercase letter (https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/57554#discussion_r266204062).

> > Also I'd like to keep the `extraConfig` escape hatch.
> 
> I'd rather not if possible, because then we have problem of not being able to merge values set in `extraConfig` with all other values, there are essentially two incompatible ways of specifying configuration then.
> [...]
> If the user really doesn't want to use the modular `config`, what I suggest instead is to have a `configFile` option as an escape hatch

The advantage of extraConfig is that the user can keep a standard format config file around (which can also be used outside of nixos) and just import that with `readFile`. But nix can still set some options, e.g. when another module needs to do some configuration on this module.

That mostly makes sense for rc-type configs, less for json I guess.

On the other hand, JSON can actually be imported with `fromJSON`…

Ideally, declarative config formats could be parsed and merged, but for imperative configs indeed `extraConfig` makes sense.

This pull request has been mentioned on **Nix community**. There might be relevant details there:

https://discourse.nixos.org/t/open-for-nomination-rfc-0042-nixos-config-options/2538/1
@danbst Yes I've thought about this too, I like the idea. However it doesn't have much to do with this RFC and as far as I can see is orthogonal to it. Feel free to open another RFC for that.
Howdy, I'm happy to be part of the shepherd team for this PR. In general I'm finding it a good idea and intend to read it carefully on the weekend and will then add comments.

>Documentation for the configuration settings will not be available in the central NixOS manual, instead the upstream documentation has to be used, which can be unfamiliar and harder to read.

I'd like to emphasize this as a serious drawback. As a NixOS user with little experience of advanced Linux configuration before starting to use NixOS, I have always been very happy to be able to simply browse http://nixos.org/nixos/options.html and discover the various things that I could easily configure (and their default), all documented consistently (even if sometimes too scarcely).

An additional, unmentioned, drawback of this proposal is that while there will be functions that will automatically turn Nix values into config files, it will be the job of the user alone to guess how to translate JSON or INI style configuration to Nix. This shouldn't be too hard to do given how close Nix is to these various configuration languages (with sets, lists, etc.) but nonetheless, it can be an additional entry barrier when starting with NixOS.

Therefore, while this proposal is good for module writers and maintainers, as it should ease their lives and make it easier to contribute, it is less good for users, especially beginners. As a trade-off, I think that this RFC should encourage module maintainers to provide options for the most-used configuration settings nonetheless (especially for widely used modules), leaving the flexibility that this proposal brings to the more arcane and advanced settings, or modules.

@Zimmi48 That's a good point, thanks for the feedback. I'll incorporate something like this into the RFC.

Edit: Addressed in https://github.com/NixOS/rfcs/pull/42/commits/9e37c0e3f0d214880634ecb65e5e1642a99cea97 and https://github.com/NixOS/rfcs/pull/42/commits/1231eaa79c5b50a72e9c633cd67c4d924fb912bc

>To play devils advocate. It seems to me that this problem could be mitigated by the module asserting that the package version lies within a supported range. Assuming you have the time to figure out the allowable ranges… 🙂

It is hard to predict, at least the future: statements about future versions are liable to be too optimistic, so each bump would require a full module review. Not realistic yet, I guess.

I must confess that I don't like this idea at all.

IMHO the biggest advantages of NixOS modules are:
 - type-safety of the options
 - mandatory documentation of all options
 - evaluation time errors for incorrect config
 - up-to-date options as soon as packages get updated

From my time when I was using puppet not having these was some of the larger problems (same goes for ansible, salt, etc.) and this RFC feels as if it is going into that direction.

The problem being addressed here is that of maintenance burden of having to update the module when the package is updated, i.e. upstream updates their config format.
That means if we were to implement this we would move that burden to each and every user of the module => If I have say ~30-40 types of machines in a NixOps network, I have to keep track of all updates to software of modules and adapt my config without any support from the NixOS modules at eval time. This RFC mentions the possibility of build-time config checking, but tools for that only exist for a small subset of software for which we have modules and some of these config checking tools need to be run on the target host in the normal runtime environment of the software (see for this the lengthy discussions on nginx config checking). So in practice most deploys would result in breakage at deployment time vs evaluation time if the config is not adapted correctly.

I very much feel that we shouldn't go down that route and feel we should reject this RFC.

One positive note though, I feel structured attrs for configs as proposed still are preferable to the current `extraConfig`.

I think we do sometimes have discussions whether some exotic option should be included into the module. In such cases, the approach of this RFC is much better than plain-text `extraConfig` at least. Maybe it is better to negotiate the wording about commonly used options that are provided explicitly and with documentation, but this is a better approach to `extraConfig`, and it is probably better to have this as a solid foundation for configuration files, even for the supported module options.

I have been mulling on this RFC for a few days and hope you don't mind some feedback from someone on the outside of the core NixOS team. :)

> Having popular/main settings as NixOS options is a good compromise. It is up to the module author to decide which options qualify for this.

This should be the RFC in a nutshell in my opinion, moving away from how it is currently leads NixOS down a path I really don't want to see it go. I am very much on @Zimmi48 and @globin's side on this. I explicitly use NixOS for the configuration options, and would think that this is one of the major draws to NixOS.

> you write a specification of the desired configuration of your system in NixOS’s modular language, and **NixOS takes care of making it happen**. [emphasis mine]

I feel this RFC if accepted wholesale moves NixOS away from one of its core goals. Yes, there is a burden on the maintainers on writing modules for users, but the burden must come somewhere and with NixOS it doesn't land on the users to figure out what options exist. I do agree that it would be better than the plain-text `extraConfig` that some packages have, but not replacing the options.

> When upstream adds or removes settings, the NixOS module needs to be updated to reflect that.

What happens when a user on 18.09 wants to configure `software-x`, finds its homepage with the settings, applies them but then the version of the software included with `nixpkgs` on 18.09 is outdated? We're back to square one, but now the onus is on the user figuring out what version include what settings, _but must do this on their own_. I personally don't feel like this RFC adequately fixes this problem, I agree it is a fundamental problem, but as previously mentioned this just shifts the burden on users.

I'm :+1: for this replacing `extraConfig` etc, but am thoroughly against this replacing NixOS modules.

>I'm :+1: for this replacing `extraConfig` etc, but am thoroughly against this replacing NixOS modules.

It cannot _replace_ NixOS modules — it requires NixOS modules to function, and more or less requires many options to be provided in the old way (otherwise things just won't work without proper defaults). Advising that the commonly configured options are provided could be stronger worded than it is in the current version, that's true.

Maybe also say that all the options used in NixOS tests should always be provided as direct options?

For less common options I would expect a user that considers setting such an option to understand the meaning of the option strictly better than the module maintainer. Figuring out that the module provides an option but handles its wrong is also a burden on the user, by the way…
I'd like to nominate @nbp

@globin Of course it would be nice if we could have documentation for every setting of every program entirely centralized in our manuals, but we need to stay realistic, that's just not possible. Duplicating the documentation for every program into our manuals, making sure they're correctly formatted, have the right type, yada yada, and every time upstream changes anything you need to change the module, that's an incredible maintenance burden we just don't have the capacity for. We have thousands of package updates per month, and hundreds of NixOS modules.

While the original idea of this RFC was to keep additional options to an absolute minimum, I adjusted this to also include popular/main options later. I should rewrite the RFC summary to better reflect that, to not cause any further misunderstandings.

### Clarification for this RFC

This RFC should be seen as a foundation for configuration files for future NixOS modules, where as opposed to using a bunch of specialized options and `extraConfig`, we use a **`config` option as a base** for the program's configuration as a whole, which provides great flexibility and doesn't limit us or the user in any way. For important/popular/main settings, **specialized options can always be easily added** to make them more discoverable, which is only even possible without friction with this RFC's approach.

Module authors should however be aware that these **options can't easily be removed again**, increase the maintenance burden, increase the review time, increase potential for mistakes, cause coupling to upstream, etc. which is why we shouldn't rush it by adding a ton of options we can't really remove again, but instead approach the level of "good options for discoverability, without them causing too many problems" with care.

I'll adjust the RFC to reflect this better.

I have now reworded parts of the RFC in https://github.com/NixOS/rfcs/pull/42/commits/e9082a92e0f97613cbdc9cb40ed0f6eb5a7ccd5e to further address the community feedback given in https://github.com/NixOS/rfcs/pull/42#issuecomment-479401625, in particular [the section on additional options](https://github.com/Infinisil/rfcs/blob/config-option/rfcs/0042-config-option.md#additional-config-options).

I would like to add my comments to this RFC as someone who was very much against this RFC initially because I had many of the same thoughts as @sondr3, but have since come to fully embrace it after I realized how this RFC actually makes NixOS easier for all of us (users and developers). 

If you classify all possible settings of any given services generated configuration file into 2 categories, either a setting classified as basic or a setting classified as advanced, and then use this as a guideline for whether something should be implemented as a NixOS option vs. implemented as a config attrSet this RFC is makes perfect sense.

A basic setting would be considered anything required for a service to operate and can have no default value. An advanced setting would be something your typical user would never generally need. Most NixOS modules provide sane defaults and often times you never need to change a thing.

At this point the thread has been going on for a while and I think concrete examples provide value.

- `services.davmail` was built using this RFC as a guideline. The only option in this module (aside from `.enable` and `.config`, of course) is `.url`. The `.url` setting was added as a NixOS option because it is absolutely required for the service to run *and* there can be no default value - the user must provide a value. Other settings that were considered to be added as NixOS options but ultimately were left to be configured via `.config` include several port bindings because the module provides sane default values which will work for 95% of users. In this specific modules case the ports selected are very much so implementation details and it is unusual that a user would need to modify those ports and this could be considered an advanced setting. Another implementation detail which 95% of users will never need to consider is the `.folderSizeLimit` setting. We don't need to bog down regular users with trivial implementation details like this which in this services case generally don't matter to the user. If a user is needing to modify these settings it means they are doing something advanced and will be better off using upstream documentation than our documentation anyways.

- `services.gitea` was not built using this RFC as a guideline and the list of NixOS options is getting overwhelming for end users. Confusion between putting a setting in `extraConfig` vs. a NixOS option leads to questions like "why doesn't option XYZ exist?" There are too many implementation specific options in this module which won't be used by 95% of users, and the 5% that do use them have very specialized needs (ie. advanced setting required). For example the `.repositoryRoot` option has a perfectly fine default value and would only ever need to be changed by an advanced user doing something out of the ordinary. This setting would be better suited living in a `.config` attrSet where advanced users could make use of it. Regular users never even need to know this setting (which is truly an implementation detail) even exists.

> you write a specification of the desired configuration of your system in NixOS’s modular language, and **NixOS takes care of making it happen**. [emphasis from @sondr3] 

What a fantastic quote that highlights how this RFC really plays into what many of us love about the module system: as users we don't want to know about/care about trivial implementation details. Next time you write a module consider if the options you are adding are implementation details which 95% of users don't even care about and if so use this RFC as a guideline :+1:

@Infinisil
> This RFC aims to solve these problems by encouraging NixOS module authors to provide a `config` option as a base for specifying program configurations with great flexibility. A set of utility functions for writing these options conveniently will be added and the documentation will be updated to recommend this way of writing modules that do program configuration.

I'm not a fan of the idea of minimizing module options, even with the emphasis of the RFC changed to just *encouraging* that, but I think the `config` option and related ideas are all good, regardless. I do personally prefer comprehensive modules, but having a minimal module is better than none. These utilities would also be useful when dealing with services where you cannot reasonably provide a comprehensive set of configuration options, for one reason or another.

Opinions on the RFC text:
1) If the suggested `config` option utilities are written, doesn't that in itself solve most of the issues around "Upstream adds a setting", even with having individual options for existing settings?
2) That module authors have to synchronize module options with upstream changes is an *advantage*, in my eyes, because it can help to insulate downstream users from changes.
   Even when it doesn't, it at least can prevent users from updating to a newer version of the daemon/service while using an old and incompatible configuration, which is fantastic... if the module maintainers have updated the module for the changed settings.
   Which raises the larger problem: I don't think there is a general way to detect module option vs. program setting mis-matches when software versions change. We can write NixOS tests, of course, but that is not *usually* a viable approach in the face of the combinatorial explosion of possible configurations. Although it may be enough for a proportion of programs, especially if they offer the ability to validate/test their configuration files as mentioned. Does anyone have any ideas on improving this situation?
3) Given the performance aspect was debunked, does "option bloat" carry problems beyond inflating the size (and intimidating-ness) of the documentation? If it does not, maybe consider a setting that flags module options as "advanced", and thus de-emphasized, folded, or otherwise 'politely hidden' in some way in the documentation?
4) Is using `nullOr` really a problem? We could use a couple of standard helpers to make working with nullable options nicer, but I haven't run into any problems aside from that.
5) I don't think removing a module option is as problematic as stated. Yes, it does annoy some people, but they'll see the breakage at eval time, well before it can affect anything running.
   Having to *unexpectedly* spend some time adapting module configuration is aggravating, but in the worst case one can always point their NixOS configuration to the older versions of that module and package, and just deal with the updates for them later.
   Correspondingly, I don't think backwards-compatibility of module options should be a high priority. Maybe instead provide a friendlier wrapper around using `disabledModules` in conjunction with importing older module and package versions? I think that explicitly providing backwards-compatibility in the module implementations runs directly counter to your goal of lowering the burden of module maintenance...
6) Why do you suggest that assertions should not be used for "things that make the service fail to start anyways"? I would have thought they would be prime candidates, as moving run-time failures to eval-time is extremely helpful to users.

## TL;DR
I think the vast majority of this RFC is really good, except:
- Comprehensive module options should not be discouraged, but definitely should be built on top of the suggested `config` mechanism.
- Backwards-compatibility of module options is not that important; NixOS already provides a mechanism for utilising older versions of modules (although it could be nicer), and eval-time failures aren't generally disruptive.


-------


@aanderse
> `services.gitea` was not built using this RFC as a guideline and the list of NixOS options is getting overwhelming for end users. Confusion between putting a setting in `extraConfig` vs. a NixOS option leads to questions like "why doesn't option XYZ exist?" There are too many implementation specific options in this module which won't be used by 95% of users, and the 5% that do use them have very specialized needs (ie. advanced setting required). For example the `.repositoryRoot` option has a perfectly fine default value and would only ever need to be changed by an advanced user doing something out of the ordinary. This setting would be better suited living in a `.config` attrSet where advanced users could make use of it. Regular users never even need to know this setting (which is truly an implementation detail) even exists.

Ironically, `services.gitea.repositoryRoot` is a **not** a good example of an option that could be left out. If it were not implemented as a NixOS option and instead left to the user to configure via `config`, it would require a much more in-depth understanding of the module's behaviour, as well as some method of removing-and-replacing [parts of the `preStart` script](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/3956a8421f2d78bc66ad9d3c23a3b5510bc695be/nixos/modules/services/misc/gitea.nix#L307-L316).

> Ironically, `services.gitea.repositoryRoot` is a **not** a good example of an option that could be left out. If it were not implemented as a NixOS option and instead left to the user to configure via `config`, it would require a much more in-depth understanding of the module's behaviour, as well as some method of removing-and-replacing [parts of the `preStart` script](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/blob/3956a8421f2d78bc66ad9d3c23a3b5510bc695be/nixos/modules/services/misc/gitea.nix#L307-L316).

@Shados I stand by my position this setting would be better suited as an advanced setting, hidden under a config attrSet. The module can give a default value for the setting and still operate on it in the preStart script with almost no modification. Given the setting has a sane default I ask why a user would ever need to change it? If the user needs to change it they are doing something I consider advanced. Yes the advanced user may need to read the module code, but I argue often times enough advanced users do anyways and we should expect advanced users to be able to do so anyways. I would appreciate more details into why you think we couldn't replace `cfg.documentRoot` with `cfg.config.documentRoot` in the preStart script. If typing is truly an issue an assertion is always possible for the select few advanced settings which are actually used inside the module.

> Backwards-compatibility of module options is not that important; NixOS already provides a mechanism for utilising older versions of modules (although it could be nicer), and eval-time failures aren't generally disruptive.

@Shados I ask that you reconsider your position here as well. As a user of NixOS in a corporate environment stability is of very high value to me. I'm definitely not against changing things up but I ask that care be taken when changes are made and generally with advanced warning. Since NixOS has such a rapid release cycle I think using module warnings or release notes to inform users of breaking changes which will be made in the next release. I'm not saying this is required in every case, but please do use discretion with these types of changes or NixOS has zero chance of succeeding in large corporate environments.

I think the declarations won't help; the options that will keep working consistently are ones that are really unavoidable for the module to do anything useful, and ones covered by NixOS tests. Everything else will get broken and fixed on upgrades; hopefully the fixes will not take too long…

@Shados Comprehensive modules are nice, but bloated modules aren't nice, as mentioned in the expanded section, a balance should be approached that has just enough options to be enough for most usecases. Over time we may add more options to approach this slowly, because we can't remove them easily again.

On your points:
1. Yeah new options in upstream doesn't conflict at all with individual options for settings.
2. With this RFC, module authors still can synchronize the module with upstream changes, see [this section](https://github.com/Infinisil/rfcs/blob/config-option/rfcs/0042-config-option.md#backwards-compatibility-for-configuration-settings). This RFC just changes the *default state* from "module unfixably broken when upstream removes an option" to "the NixOS user can at least fix it themselves"
3. The point "Timeconsuming to implement, tedious to review and hard to maintain" in [this section](https://github.com/Infinisil/rfcs/blob/config-option/rfcs/0042-config-option.md#single-option-for-every-setting) still stands. I am one of the main reviewers of NixOS modules, and modules with a lot of options are a pain tbh. My free time to review is limited.
4. `nullOr` is not very nice because you don't really know what `null` represents and if you know it represents the default, you don't know what the default is. Is `null` itself the default? What about settings that have a default of 10, but could also be unset, does null in the module system represent the default or the unset value? It's just mehh.
5. Very much disagree. Keeping backwards compatibility is important, we don't want to break everybody's config every release. The `mkRemovedOptionModule` function doesn't take a string argument for the explanation of the removal for no reason. I really don't want to put "The option was deemed not important enough" in there. If people see an option in the manual, they expect to be able to use it without problems. And the `disabledModule` hack is really ugly, I don't want to force that on people any more than I have to already.
6. Because we can't protect against everything that the program might deem as fail-worthy, this would lead to 100 of ugly assertions that may be buggy themselves. People can get an error at runtime instead and fix their config accordingly, which is not a problem. This is why I suggested to only use assertions when it's a failure you don't really see at runtime and is hard to detect. We can't and we don't need to have NixOS be an all-knowing oracle that knows about every single thing that might fail at runtime, it's just not possible, there's too much complexity and variation.

tl;dr:

- Backwards compatibility is important and we shouldn't ignore it
- Eval failures instead of runtime failures are nice, but we can't protect against everything. We should reserve using the tedious to implement assertions for things that you wouldn't see at runtime. And every assertion again adds a bit of the disadvantages mentioned in the RFC.

@aanderse > I stand by my position this setting would be better suited as an advanced setting, hidden under a config attrSet. I think perhaps I am missing something here? To me the suggested approach seems largely identical to making it an explicit module option, except that you do not documentation (and type checking, unless you have equivalent assertions) on it. The work required to implement is nearly as much, and the maintenance burden remains (any upstream change to the program setting would still require module maintainer intervention). Anecdotally, I do happen to use this option, as well as similar ones in many other modules, in order to store important state data in a single location[1](#foot1). Unnecessary documentation may arguably be more of a maintenance burden than it is worth, but in this case it serves a dual purpose in helping to clarify the intent of the Nix code that uses it. > I ask that you reconsider your position here as well. As a user of NixOS in a corporate environment stability is of very high value to me. My point of view is not that breaking backwards-compatibility *in general* is OK, but that it is OK specifically if the breakage is surfaced at eval-time. In relation to this RFC: I think using `config` for most options can only ever be *equally or less stable* than using more comprehensive module options, never more stable (in the sense of breaking something at run-time). To elucidate this, consider how a worst-case scenario would be handled with each method. Worst-case meaning that deprecation warnings are absent (or just missed by the user) and that NixOS tests did not catch the issue. A new software version can basically introduce two types of breaking change; either it removes a feature (and its corresponding setting(s)), or it changes a setting, but it still exists (renamed, moved, type change, etc.). If the setting has a module option: If the module maintainers do not notice the issue before it gets to you, you end up with a run-time failure. If they do, you end up with either no failures (e.g. if only the setting name changed, the maintainer may keep the option name the same) or an eval-time failure (e.g. if there is some semantic change to the setting, then the option name, type, or assertions would have changed). If the setting is only exposed through `config`: You get a run-time failure. Of course with the proposed `config` rather than `extraConfig`, theoretically the module maintainer could still notice the issue and either take the `fixedUpConfig` approach for a non-semantic change (arguably with increased maintenance burden over the module option approach), or provide an assertion that checks for use of the old `config` sub-attribute and warns you, meaning you get an eval-time failure. That said: if non-option settings are explicitly meant to be more advanced and/or less-used, then it isn't likely they're going to get NixOS tests, deprecation warnings, or much attention from module maintainers. Not to imply that module options always do. That said, my experience with corporate clients says this is largely irrelevant to them. All the ones I have worked with employ some kind of change management for internal things, and a QA process for customer-facing things. These kinds of issues would almost certainly all be caught by these; it is more subtle things like new bugs in a fresh version of some dependency that tend to slip through the net. On that note: To my knowledge the kind of "stability" corporations usually want has more to do with software and service *versions* being very specific -- due to e.g. needing to run legacy software that is incompatible with newer versions of some things, having extremely specific/strict version requirements from a software vendor, or simply a desire to stick with the "devil you know" instead of taking the risk of new and unknown bugs by moving to a newer package version. This kind of stability is already well-handled by Nix/OS's excellent ability to pin nixpkg versions, as well as to mix package and module versions from specific nixpkg versions. The main barriers to entry I can see for Nix* in corporate environments have more to do with the availability of trusted support contracts, and in the difficulties of training staff and generally getting a handle on the Nix ecosystem. If you have a different perspective on it, I'd be interested in hearing more, but as that is less relevant to this RFC, maybe just message me on IRC if you want to discuss it further? ------- @Infinisil 2. If module options are themselves backed on `config`, then a removed or changed upstream option should no longer be "unfixably broken", no? If `config` becomes the default base for module implementations, then this problem is solved either way. 3. Fair enough. I would suggest that reviewers likely should not be doing (much) checking that "types are correct, descriptions are fitting, [and] defaults are acceptable", because this essentially requires every reviewer be familiar with the software in question. I would inherently expect the module author or maintainer to have knowledge of the software, not the reviewer. Shouldn't the review process then instead focus more on the Nix/OS aspects (whether or not the code is sane, dis/use of conventions, possible conflicts with some of NixOS' atypical configuration, etc.)? I realize there's always some overlap, but perhaps you are holding yourself and other reviewers to an unrealistic standard? Are there any explicit guidelines on the module review process currently? 4. I see your point. Would there be an issue with mandating or recommending that `nullOr` is only used where `null` is a meaningful value to the program, and options must always have a default set? The default could fall "out of sync" with the upstream default program setting, but: - It isn't exactly uncommon for distros to set different defaults than upstream, so I don't think this is necessarily problematic[2](#foot2). - Otherwise, this isn't really any different to the existing possibility of the option name or semantics falling out of sync with the upstream program, and that price is already being paid if a module option is being used. 5. I think I should lay out my position a bit more clearly. Primarily, I don't think that removing a module option for *a program setting that was actually removed* (as in the underlying feature is gone) is a problem. Yes, `mkRemovedOptionModule` should definitely be used in these cases, and yes, a user of the option will likely need to change something about their config. But the only ways to avoid that in this case is either for the module to somehow re-implement the removed function[3](#foot3), or to delay the package update and give a deprecation warning, which just postpones the problem. In cases where an upstream setting has had a purely syntactical or otherwise trivial change, I am in favour of transparent backwards-compatibility, either by simply changing the implementation of a module option, or by your suggested use of some fixup helper on the `config` attribute. Although I'll note that I wouldn't expect many non-option settings to get this treatment, but it is nice that they *could*. I suggest that things like `mkRenamedOptionModule` should mainly be used when moving options between modules, or when changing the interface/design of a module, neither of which are typically done in response to upstream changes. I think for the most part this is pretty consistent with how things are already managed, although I have seen a few totally superfluous option name changes to match upstream setting name changes. My main point is that you have strongly emphasised a perceived difficulty in removing module options *in general*, and I don't think you have justified that sufficiently. I *do* see this in the case of changing the interface or design of a module, but this is both a relatively uncommon occurrence, and also much more frequently done to NixOS abstract system modules (like networking) than to specific program/software modules. The `config` idea isn't generally applicable to the former type of module. 6. That makes sense, maybe add something along those lines in the RFC text? ------ 1: In order to simplify backup procedures, host under a specific mount point, etc. `/var/lib` is less useful for this, because it is also full of state data from services that do not need to be backed up or treated specially. [↩](#ref1) 2: Conceivably a change in a default upstream value could be very important, but I would expect that to be fairly rare. [↩](#ref2) 3: Which may occasionally be possible, but almost certainly carries an undesirable complexity and maintenance burden. [↩](#ref3)

@Shados upon reading the source code of the entire module in more depth I'm still not convinced that *must* be a module option... but your comments saying "bad example" in are correct as the `repositoryRoot` isn't nearly as clear as the `disableRegistration` option I believe. Thanks for pointing that out.

So this PR really consists of two parts, I'd like to talk a bit more about the intention of them:

### Part 1

Using `config` options of an appropriate type for program configurations instead of stringly-typed `extraConfig` options where applicable, increasing modularity and allowing overriding of all settings.

### Part 2

Since with part 1 there are no more hardcoded defaults and people can set any option they want in a composable way, there is no need to change nixpkgs anymore for options that aren't in the module, so people don't need to make a PR if they need a certain option that's not (yet?) supported.

This also means that module authors don't need to add every single option they need, but can instead decide on a "most important" set of options to encode as NixOS options, the ones which they deem to be useful for most people, while deferring the less important ones to the `config` option, for more advanced users who need special settings. Previously you couldn't do any of that, because the stringly-typed approach would restrict you to only the settings available through NixOS options.

This way, we can keep our NixOS options as useful as possible for everybody. This might give us 10 options for some service, where people can go and say "I'm glad I have a nice overview of the most important customizations to this service". They can scroll through `man configuration.nix` and see all options within a couple key presses.

In contrast are modules with 100 options where almost all people only use 10% of them because the others are really only useful in special cases. And the more options a module has, the harder it is to see the useful ones.

I'd rather have people spend more time making modules more high-quality by documenting a small option set properly, working out quirks with different interactions and thinking about what options would benefit most users, instead of just dumping a whole bunch of options. Quality over quantity.

---

The controversy arising here lies in part 2 only. I can split part 2 from this RFC, but I think it goes hand in hand with part 1, and I hope above explanation gives you some insight as to why I think it's a good idea.

In preparation for the RFC meeting on Monday a short summary of the discussion:
* Generally accepted point of this RFC is **preferring a NixOS attrset option `config`** or similar **to a block of text in `extraConfig`, `configFile`** etc., with the loudest criticism there being, that upstream config samples cannot be pasted into the NixOS config verbatim.
* Composability (merging)?
* **Documentation** is seen as a larger issue by a number of people, with more options available, there is a central place where it can be viewed for all services (NixOS website, `man configuration.nix`, locally built webpage) and it contains the type, the default value and an example besides the description, which upstream doesn't always offer. OTOH our descriptions might not always be as comprehensive and elaborate as they should be.
* Furthermore we mandate adding **types** to module options which is way harder to achieve with only a `config` option
* With this in mind therefore we generally have more **evaluation errors**, rather than **runtime errors**, due to typing restrictions in modules, also typos in option names currently are evaluation errors, therefore a user mostly has issues prior to deployment and not when deployed causing downtime
* A big motivation of this RFC is to **reduce workload of the module maintainer(s) and reviewers** by reducing the options, i.e. having to adapt/remove options when the package is updated. This generally is undisputed but from this the problem arises that this **maintenance is shifted to each user of the module** who has to check for all packages being updated, if they need to adapt their configuration on every rebuild. Currently this would have led to eval errors rather than runtime errors as mentioned above. This also might cause an increase in issues from users that wish to have help with their software configuration.
* This leads to the discussion on **backward compatibility**, for renamed/changed options either `mkRenamedOption` or other means hidden in the implementation can be used currently, similarly this can be done in the implementation with this RFC (priorities might become an issue if both the new and the old option are used in this case, though). Upstream-removed options can be removed if they are `mkOption`'ed , not in `config` -> eval error vs runtime error
* the point on PRs with a **lot of options being harder to review**, has been addressed in a comment, that reviewers should be **encouraged to check more for Nix(OS)-specific issues, rather than software-specific issues**, and that be left more to the actual maintainers of the package and module.
* **`mkDefault`'ed option values** as being advertised in the RFC **do not show up in the documentation** and cannot be easily added to it due to them generally be guarded behind at least `mkIf cfg.enable`.
* **config-checking** via tools can sometimes only be run in the correct environment (e.g. search discussions wrt nginx config checking). This can be worked-around by running in `preStart`, although resulting in a runtime error. Also this can cause issues with cross-compiling (https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/62853). This workaround assumes that the config passed, is valid for the default package version used in the module (can cause issues with packages with different versions/implementations due to different available options)
* `types.attrs` currently **naively merges** with `//`in contrast to the **elaborate merging capabilities with priorities provided for module options**. This reduces composability and possibilities to work with the configuration options of one module at another place (abstracting module, dependant, etc.)

**Warning, private opinion ahead**
I have tried to summarise the discussion objectively, please refer to the RFC itself for more elaboration on the motivation and ideas of some points, where I have been brief above.
Personally I still don't like the approach of this RFC trying to discourage more options. I firmly believe that we should be handling the maintenance of changes needed to module config rather than users. This reduces the sum of work for everyone and hopefully users who notice issues will more easily work with us rather than everyone having to find a solution themselves. I especially think that our documentation generated from our module options is outstanding and very nice for beginners who generally don't want to search around in diverse upstream documentation, having to find the right version of the documentation fitting to the package version we are shipping. Also I love eval errors over runtime errors so much, NixOS version updates for ~50 servers running a whole range of different software mostly is just fixing eval errors until that succeeds again and then hardly any runtime errors occur. Otherwise I'd have to check each and every software for upgrades and incompatibilities in its configuration, in the current state this is crowd-sourced in nix and hardly any downtime due to changed configuration ever happens. 

I'd propose changing this RFC to just prefer a `config` attrs to `extraConfig` and not discourage adding options. I prefer having a module with a few options and an escape hatch in `config` to no module. Also I prefer having a module with a lot of options to one with only a few. Abstractions are good (`enableACME` and `forceSSL` in nginx come to mind) and an escape hatch with `config` or similar should also always be included IMHO.

yorick on IRC raises the concern that sometimes it's good to be able to "steal" the generated config from a module for reuse somewhere else (perhaps outside of NixOS). This is another good reason for having a `configFile` option, which contains the final path of the configuration file. This can then be used to both get the final config and set it (override the generated one). Why `configFile` and not `configText`/`configString`? `configFile` is more flexible because it allows you to:
- Set it to a stateful location like `/var/lib/foo/config.json` if needed
- Set it to a derivation that checks the configuration first (as described [here](https://github.com/Infinisil/rfcs/blob/config-option/rfcs/0042-config-option.md#configuration-checking))
- Makes it obvious that no merging will be happening. You can't set a file path more than once, whereas you could do it (if the type allows it) with `configText`. No merging should be happening because strings can't merge with the structured `settings` options.

This shouldn't be integral to this RFC, but I'll probably add a note on `configFile`/`configText` to it because it fits here.

@edolstra Yeah that's a good point. Maybe making `configFile` readonly and forcing people to use the modular `settings` option is the way forward. As already mentioned in https://github.com/NixOS/rfcs/pull/42#issuecomment-475873999, people can even still assign stringly config's for which there is a config type -> nix value parser available.

However I still feel like there would be a significant amount of people wanting to have a settable `configFile` option. Having to convert big configs to Nix values can be a pain. By providing a settable `configFile` option, the entry into NixOS might be significantly lowered for a lot of people because they can easily migrate from their non-NixOS machines.

An argument for a stateful `configFile` value like `"/var/lib/foo/config"` is that NixOS rebuilds [are slow](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/issues/57477). When I need to debug some program or fine-tune some program, it would be very nice if I could escape from the slow `nixos-rebuild` for a moment.

Another argument for a stateful `configFile` is that a lot of applications have a built-in GUI to edit the config, which can be a whole lot more convenient than having to edit `configuration.nix`. These wouldn't work with a non-stateful `configFile`. And oftentimes people would rather give up some reproducibility than to lose a convenient GUI.

> While using an attribute set greatly improves readability, this might cause issues in cases where the order of the arguments matters.

Indeed, that's one reason why it supports lists. You can pass a list of single-attribute sets if you require full control over the ordering, or you can order only those arguments where it matters.

> -foo is serialised to -foo and bar to --bar

What's the alternative? The idea here is that an option _name_ can't start with a dash by definition, so the function takes an initial dash as a signal that the user has already taken care of this part. 

Some programs take their long arguments with only a single dash; changing `-foo` into `--foo` would be odd (why didn't the user just provide `foo` in the first place?) and would make it impossible to actually pass `-foo` to the program without resorting to raw strings.

+# Summary
+[summary]: #summary
+
+A lot of NixOS options exist to specify single settings of configuration files. Along with such options come multiple disadvantages, such as having to synchronize with upstream changes, option bloat and more. An alternative is to provide options for passing the configuration as a string, such as the common `configFile` or `extraConfig` options, but this also comes with a set of disadvantages, including difficulty to override values and bad modularity.
+
+This RFC proposes aims to solve these problems by encouraging NixOS module authors to provide an option for specifying the programs configuration file as a Nix value, providing a set of utility functions for writing these options conveniently, and updating the documentation to recommend this way of doing program configuration.
+
+# Motivation
+[motivation]: #motivation
+
+NixOS commonly has 2 models of specifying configuration for programs, each with their own set of problems. This RFC aims to solve all of them.
+
+## Single option for every setting
+
+Having a single option for every setting in the configuration file, this often gets combined with an `extraConfig` option to provide greater flexibility. Problems:
+
+- Coupling to upstream
+  - When upstream adds or removes settings, the NixOS module needs to be updated to reflect that.
+    - Upstream adds a setting: If the module has an `extraConfig` option people might set the new setting there. But if we ever add it as a NixOS option, we'll have trouble merging the values together with what the user already specified in `extraConfig`
+    - Upstream removes a setting (backwards incompatible): The NixOS module is straight up broken in nixpkgs until somebody fixes it, end users can't fix it themselves (unless the module provides a `configFile` option which can override the generated one)

+# Summary
+[summary]: #summary
+
+A lot of NixOS options exist to specify single settings of configuration files. Along with such options come multiple disadvantages, such as having to synchronize with upstream changes, option bloat and more. An alternative is to provide options for passing the configuration as a string, such as the common `configFile` or `extraConfig` options, but this also comes with a set of disadvantages, including difficulty to override values and bad modularity.
+
+This RFC proposes aims to solve these problems by encouraging NixOS module authors to provide an option for specifying the programs configuration file as a Nix value, providing a set of utility functions for writing these options conveniently, and updating the documentation to recommend this way of doing program configuration.
+
+# Motivation
+[motivation]: #motivation
+
+NixOS commonly has 2 models of specifying configuration for programs, each with their own set of problems. This RFC aims to solve all of them.
+
+## Single option for every setting
+
+Having a single option for every setting in the configuration file, this often gets combined with an `extraConfig` option to provide greater flexibility. Problems:
+
+- Coupling to upstream
+  - When upstream adds or removes settings, the NixOS module needs to be updated to reflect that.
+    - Upstream adds a setting: If the module has an `extraConfig` option people might set the new setting there. But if we ever add it as a NixOS option, we'll have trouble merging the values together with what the user already specified in `extraConfig`
+    - Upstream removes a setting (backwards incompatible): The NixOS module is straight up broken in nixpkgs until somebody fixes it, end users can't fix it themselves (unless the module provides a `configFile` option which can override the generated one)
+  - The documentation of the upstream settings needs to be copied over to the NixOS options, which means it might get out of sync with changes

+  - It takes a non-zero amount of time to write all the wanted options out into a NixOS module

+- [#52096](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/52096)

+[motivation]: #motivation
+
+NixOS commonly has 2 models of specifying configuration for programs, each with their own set of problems. This RFC aims to solve all of them.
+

+

+
+- Coupling to upstream
+  - When upstream adds or removes settings, the NixOS module needs to be updated to reflect that.
+    - Upstream adds a setting: If the module has an `extraConfig` option people might set the new setting there. But if we ever add it as a NixOS option, we'll have trouble merging the values together with what the user already specified in `extraConfig`

+  - The documentation of the upstream settings needs to be copied over to the NixOS options, which means it might get out of sync with changes
+  - The upstream defaults are being copied to the NixOS modules, so we need to also update the defaults whenever upstream changes them. This can be solved by using `nullOr` to allow for a `null` value to indicate that the upstream default shall be used, but that's not very nice.
+- Option bloat: <s>NixOS evaluation time is still linear in the number of *available* options for all users, even though everybody only uses a fraction of them. +- Timeconsuming to implement, tedious to review and hard to maintain
+  - It takes a non-zero amount of time to write all the wanted options out into a NixOS module
+  - Reviewing is tedious because people need to make sure types are correct, descriptions are fitting, defaults are acceptable, for every option added. Due to the size and repetitiveness, people are also less willing to thoroughly review the code.
+  - The bigger the NixOS module is the harder it is to maintain, and the less people want to actually maintain it. 
+- Responsibility for backwards compatibility: By adding such options, we obligate ourselves to handle backwards incompatibilites on our side. We will have to support these options for a long time and can't remove them without at least one person being annoyed about it.
+
+## `configFile` or `extraConfig` option
+
+An option for specifying the contents of the configuration file directly with `configFile` or `extraConfig`. Problems:
+
+- Not very modular at all
+  - In case of json or a `configFile` option, you can only assign the option once, merging is impossible
+  - In case of ini (or similar), assigning a single option multiple times to make use of list concatenation, ordering or priorities is impossible, so in general you can't e.g. override a default value set somewhere else.
+- No syntax checking: Users will have to know the syntax of the configuration language and encode their values properly, any syntax error will only be realized when the program errors at runtime.
+
+## Occurences of problems
+
+- Because prometheus uses options to encode every possible setting, [#56017](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/56017) is needed to allow users to set a part of the configuration that wasn't encoded yet.
+- Because strongswan-ctl uses options to encode its full configuration, changes like [#49197](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/49197) are needed to update our options with upstream changes.
+- Pull requests like [#57036](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/57036) or [#38324](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/38324) are needed because users wish to have more configuration options than the ones provided.
+
+## Previous discussions
+
+- https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/44923#issuecomment-412393196
+- https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/55957#issuecomment-464561483 -> https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/57716
+
+## Implementations
+
+This idea has been implemented already in some places:
+- [#45470](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/45470)
+- [#52096](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/52096)
+- [My Murmur module](https://github.com/Infinisil/system/blob/45c3ea36651a2f4328c8a7474148f1c5ecb18e0a/config/new-modules/murmur.nix)
+
+# Detailed design
+[design]: #detailed-design
+
+For specifying configuration files to programs in NixOS options, there should be a main single option called `config` which represents the configuration of the program as a Nix value, which can then be converted to the configuration file format the program expects. This may look as follows:
+
+```nix
+{ config, lib, ... }: with lib;
+let
+
+  cfg = config.services.foo;
+  
+  # Use port specified in config or the upstream default otherwise
+  # Needed to open the correct port
+  port = cfg.config.port or 2546;
+  
+  configText = configGen.json cfg.config;
+  
+in {
+
+  options.services.foo = {
+    enable = mkEnableOption "foo service";
+    
+    config = mkOption {
+      type = lib.types.config.json;
+      default = {};
+      description = ''
+        Configuration for foo. Refer to <link xlink:href="https://example.com/docs/foo"\>
+        for documentation on the supported values.
+      '';
+    };
+  };
+  
+  config = mkIf cfg.enable {
+  
+    # Set minimal config to get service working by default
+    services.foo.config = {
+      dataPath = "/var/lib/foo";
+      logLevel = mkDefault "WARN";
+    };
+  
+    environment.etc."foo.json".text = configText;
+    
+    networking.firewall.allowedTCPPorts = [ port ];
+    # ...
+  };
+}
+```

+- Ability to easily query arbitrary configuration values with `nix-instantiate --eval '<nixpkgs/nixos>' -A config.services.foo.config`
+- The configuration file is well formatted with the right amount of indentation everywhere
+- Usually hardcoded defaults can now be replaced by simple assignment of the `config` option, which also allows people to override those values with `mkForce`
+
+*: The only problem it doesn't solve is the coupling to upstream defaults for options that need to be known at evaluation time, such as `port` in the example above, but that's not really avoidable.
+
+### Configuration types
+
+A set of types for common configuration formats should be provided in `lib.types.config`. Such a type should encode what values can be set in files of this configuration format as a Nix value, with the module system being able to merge multiple values correctly. This is the part that checks whether the user set an encodeable value. This can be extended over time, but could include the following as a start:
+- JSON
+- YAML, which is probably the same as JSON
+- INI
+- A simple `key=value` format
+- A recursive `key.subkey.subsubkey=value` format
+
+Sometimes programs have their own configuration formats, in which case the type should be implemented in the program's module directly.
+
+### Configuration format writers
+
+To convert the Nix value into the configuration string, a set of configuration format writers should be provided under `lib.config`. These should make sure that the resulting text is somewhat properly formatted with readable indentation. These writers will have to include ones for all of the above-mentioned configuration types. As with the type, if the program has its own configuration format, the writer should be implemented in its module directly.
+
+### Documentation
+
+The nixpkgs manual should be updated to recommend this way of doing program configuration in modules, along with examples.
+
+## Limitations
+
+- Limited to configuration file formats representable conveniently in Nix, such as JSON, YAML, INI, key-value files, or similar formats. Examples of unsuitable configuration formats are Haskell, Lisp, Lua or other generic programming languages. For those it is recommended to not hardcode anything and provide a `config` option with type `types.str` or `types.lines` if it makes sense to merge multiple assignments of it.
+
+## Additional config options
+Sometimes it makes sense to have an additional NixOS option for a specific configuration setting. In general this should be discussed on a case-by-case basis to judge whether it makes sense. However keep in mind that it's always possible to add more options later on, but you can't as easily remove existing options. Instances of where it can make sense are:
+- Settings that are necessary for the module to work and are different for every user, so they can't have a default. Examples are `services.dd-agent.api_key`, `services.davmail.url` or `services.hydra.hydraURL`. Having a separate option for these settings can give a much better error message when you don't set them (instead of failing at runtime or having to encode the requirement in an assertion) and better discoverability.
+- Password settings: Some programs configuration files require passwords in them directly. Since we try to avoid having passwords in the Nix store, it is advisable to provide a `passwordFile` option as well, which would replace a placeholder password in the configuration file at runtime.

+

+
+- Limited to configuration file formats representable conveniently in Nix, such as JSON, YAML, INI, key-value files, or similar formats. +Sometimes it makes sense to have an additional NixOS option for a specific configuration setting. In general this should be discussed on a case-by-case basis to judge whether it makes sense. +
+  options.services.foo = {
+    # ...
+    
+    domain = mkOption {
+      type = types.str;
+      description = "Domain this service operates on.";
+    };
+  };
+  
+  config = mkIf cfg.enable {
+    services.foo.config = {
+      # ...
+      domain = mkDefault cfg.domain;
+    };
+  };

+```
+
+Even though we have two ways of specifying this configuration setting now, the user is free to choose either way.

+- Types of configuration settings can't be checked*, which can lead to packages failing at runtime instead of evaluation time. If the program supports a mode for checking its configuration, this problem can be solved elegantly by using it.

review_comments.body:
I think this very much depends on the program's configuration format. For example it would be more confusing than helpful to add some semi-hardcoded default string to xmonad's Haskell configuration format, I'd rather just have a `config` option for that without any specialized NixOS options.

And with Bash it makes both sense to have semi-hardcoded defaults (stuff like `HISTFILE=${cfg.histFile}`) which you can always override later on anyways, and a `types.lines` option with which you can add arbitrary commands.

The only reason I can think of that a bunch of NixOS options, *without* a `types.lines` option are reasonable is when the program is configured with a programming language, when it wouldn't actually have needed to be a programming language, because the configuration is so simple.

+  };

+
+A set of types for common configuration formats should be provided in `lib.types.config`. Such a type should encode what values can be set in files of this configuration format as a Nix value, with the module system being able to merge multiple values correctly. This is the part that checks whether the user set an encodeable value. This can be extended over time, but could include the following as a start:
+- JSON
+- YAML, which is probably the same as JSON
+- INI
+- A simple `key=value` format
+- A recursive `key.subkey.subsubkey=value` format
+
+Sometimes programs have their own configuration formats, in which case the type should be implemented in the program's module directly.

+
+The nixpkgs manual should be updated to recommend this way of doing program configuration in modules, along with examples.

+- Limited to configuration file formats representable conveniently in Nix, such as JSON, YAML, INI, key-value files, or similar formats. review_comments.body:
My thought process was that we'd only need to set values in the config file that are needed for the program to work at all. Since in this case `port` isn't needed for the program to work at all, we don't have to include it.

By setting the value in the config file, so we can access it by `cfg.config.port` directly without worry whether it exists or not, seems a bit like a bleeding interface, exposing an implementation detail. The value doesn't need to be in the config file for us to be able to open the firewall with a default value, it just makes it a tiny bit more convenient.

But then again, if our module needs the default `port`, the user might also want to access it outside of the module (e.g. if they need to use the port for a nginx proxy), which wouldn't be possible with how it is now. And in any case `let ... in`'s in modules are always a bit annoying because they're not accessible in any way from outside.

So yeah, I'll change this to `port = mkDefault 2546`, has more advantages and is simpler.

+# Summary
+[summary]: #summary
+
+A lot of NixOS options exist to specify single settings of configuration files. Along with such options come multiple disadvantages, such as having to synchronize with upstream changes, option bloat and more. An alternative is to provide options for passing the configuration as a string, such as the common `configFile` or `extraConfig` options, but this also comes with a set of disadvantages, including difficulty to override values and bad modularity.
+
+This RFC proposes aims to solve these problems by encouraging NixOS module authors to provide an option for specifying the programs configuration file as a Nix value, providing a set of utility functions for writing these options conveniently, and updating the documentation to recommend this way of doing program configuration.
+
+# Motivation
+[motivation]: #motivation
+
+NixOS commonly has 2 models of specifying configuration for programs, each with their own set of problems. This RFC aims to solve all of them.
+
+## Single option for every setting
+
+Having a single option for every setting in the configuration file, this often gets combined with an `extraConfig` option to provide greater flexibility. Problems:
+
+- Coupling to upstream
+  - When upstream adds or removes settings, the NixOS module needs to be updated to reflect that.
+    - Upstream adds a setting: If the module has an `extraConfig` option people might set the new setting there. But if we ever add it as a NixOS option, we'll have trouble merging the values together with what the user already specified in `extraConfig`
+    - Upstream removes a setting (backwards incompatible): The NixOS module is straight up broken in nixpkgs until somebody fixes it, end users can't fix it themselves (unless the module provides a `configFile` option which can override the generated one)
+  - The documentation of the upstream settings needs to be copied over to the NixOS options, which means it might get out of sync with changes
+  - The upstream defaults are being copied to the NixOS modules, so we need to also update the defaults whenever upstream changes them. This can be solved by using `nullOr` to allow for a `null` value to indicate that the upstream default shall be used, but that's not very nice.
+- Option bloat: <s>NixOS evaluation time is still linear in the number of *available* options for all users, even though everybody only uses a fraction of them. This means that when a module adds 100 new options, this leads to a direct increase in evaluation time for every `nixos-rebuild switch` of everybody using NixOS.</s> With high confidence debunked in [#57477](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/issues/57477).
+- Timeconsuming to implement, tedious to review and hard to maintain
+  - It takes a non-zero amount of time to write all the wanted options out into a NixOS module
+  - Reviewing is tedious because people need to make sure types are correct, descriptions are fitting, defaults are acceptable, for every option added. Due to the size and repetitiveness, people are also less willing to thoroughly review the code.
+  - The bigger the NixOS module is the harder it is to maintain, and the less people want to actually maintain it. 
+- Responsibility for backwards compatibility: By adding such options, we obligate ourselves to handle backwards incompatibilites on our side. We will have to support these options for a long time and can't remove them without at least one person being annoyed about it.
+
+## `configFile` or `extraConfig` option
+
+An option for specifying the contents of the configuration file directly with `configFile` or `extraConfig`. Problems:
+
+- Not very modular at all
+  - In case of json or a `configFile` option, you can only assign the option once, merging is impossible
+  - In case of ini (or similar), assigning a single option multiple times to make use of list concatenation, ordering or priorities is impossible, so in general you can't e.g. override a default value set somewhere else.
+- No syntax checking: Users will have to know the syntax of the configuration language and encode their values properly, any syntax error will only be realized when the program errors at runtime.
+
+## Occurences of problems
+
+- Because prometheus uses options to encode every possible setting, [#56017](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/56017) is needed to allow users to set a part of the configuration that wasn't encoded yet.
+- Because strongswan-ctl uses options to encode its full configuration, changes like [#49197](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/49197) are needed to update our options with upstream changes.
+- Pull requests like [#57036](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/57036) or [#38324](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/38324) are needed because users wish to have more configuration options than the ones provided.
+
+## Previous discussions
+
+- https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/44923#issuecomment-412393196
+- https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/55957#issuecomment-464561483 -> https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/57716
+
+## Implementations
+
+This idea has been implemented already in some places:
+- [#45470](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/45470)
+- [#52096](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/pull/52096)
+- [My Murmur module](https://github.com/Infinisil/system/blob/45c3ea36651a2f4328c8a7474148f1c5ecb18e0a/config/new-modules/murmur.nix)
+

+
+For specifying configuration files to programs in NixOS options, there should be a main single option called `config` which represents the configuration of the program as a Nix value, which can then be converted to the configuration file format the program expects. This may look as follows:
+
+```nix
+{ config, lib, ... }: with lib;
+let
+
+  cfg = config.services.foo;
+  
+  # Use port specified in config or the upstream default otherwise
+  # Needed to open the correct port
+  port = cfg.config.port or 2546;
+  
+  configText = configGen.json cfg.config;
+  
+in {
+
+  options.services.foo = {
+    enable = mkEnableOption "foo service";
+    
+    config = mkOption {
+      type = lib.types.config.json;
+      default = {};
+      description = ''
+        Configuration for foo. Refer to <link xlink:href="https://example.com/docs/foo"\>
+        for documentation on the supported values.
+      '';
+    };
+  };
+  
+  config = mkIf cfg.enable {
+  
+    # Set minimal config to get service working by default
+    services.foo.config = {
+      dataPath = "/var/lib/foo";
+      logLevel = mkDefault "WARN";
+    };
+  
+    environment.etc."foo.json".text = configText;
+

+    # ...
+  };
+}
+```
+

+- Ability to easily query arbitrary configuration values with `nix-instantiate --eval '<nixpkgs/nixos>' -A config.services.foo.config`
+- The configuration file is well formatted with the right amount of indentation everywhere
+- Usually hardcoded defaults can now be replaced by simple assignment of the `config` option, which also allows people to override those values with `mkForce`
+
+*: The only problem it doesn't solve is the coupling to upstream defaults for options that need to be known at evaluation time, such as `port` in the example above, but that's not really avoidable.
+
+### Configuration types
+
+A set of types for common configuration formats should be provided in `lib.types.config`. Such a type should encode what values can be set in files of this configuration format as a Nix value, with the module system being able to merge multiple values correctly. +- YAML, which is probably the same as JSON
+- INI
+- A simple `key=value` format
+- A recursive `key.subkey.subsubkey=value` format
+

+
+### Configuration format writers
+
+To convert the Nix value into the configuration string, a set of configuration format writers should be provided under `lib.config`. These should make sure that the resulting text is somewhat properly formatted with readable indentation. These writers will have to include ones for all of the above-mentioned configuration types. +
+### Documentation
+
+The nixpkgs manual should be updated to recommend this way of doing program configuration in modules, along with examples.
+
+## Limitations
+
+- Limited to configuration file formats representable conveniently in Nix, such as JSON, YAML, INI, key-value files, or similar formats. Examples of unsuitable configuration formats are Haskell, Lisp, Lua or other generic programming languages. For those it is recommended to not hardcode anything and provide a `config` option with type `types.str` or `types.lines` if it makes sense to merge multiple assignments of it.

+### Defaults
+
+Depending on how default settings matter, we need to set them differently and for different reasons:
+- If the module needs a specific value for a setting because of how the module or NixOS works (e.g. `logger = "systemd"`, because NixOS uses `systemd` for logging), then the value should *not* use `mkDefault`. This way a user can't easily override this setting (which would break the module in some way) and will have to use `mkForce` instead to change it. This also indicates that they are leaving supported territory, and will probably have to change something else to make it work again (e.g. if they set `logger = mkForce "/var/log/foo"` they'll have to change their workflow of where to look for logs).
+- If the program needs a setting to be present in the configuration file because otherwise it would fail at runtime and demand a value, the module should set this value *with* a `mkDefault` to the default upstream value, which will then be the equivalent of a starter configuration file. This allows users to easily change the value, but also enables a smooth first use of the module without having to manually set such defaults to get it to a working state. +

+    assertions = [

+  };

If a configuration checking tool is available, optimally by the program itself, it should be used if possible, as it can greatly improve user experience. The following illustrates an example of how this might look like
+
+```nix
+{ config, pkgs, lib, ... }: with lib;
+
+let
+
+  configText = configGen.json cfg.config;
+
+  configFile = pkgs.runCommand "foo-config.json" {
+    # Because this program will be run at build time, we need `nativeBuildInputs` instead of `buildInputs`
+    nativeBuildInputs = [ pkgs.foo ];
+
+    inherit configText;
+    passAsFile = [ "configText" ];
+  } ''
+    foo check-config $configTextPath
+    cp $configTextPath $out
+  '';
+
+in { /* ... */ }
+```
+
+#### Ad-hoc checks with assertions
+
+While not as optimal as a configuration checker tool, assertions can be used to add flexible ad-hoc checks for type or other properties at **evaluation time**. It should only be used to ensure important properties that break the service in ways that are otherwise hard or slow to detect (and easy to detect for the module system), not for things that make the service fail to start anyways (unless there's a good reason for it). The following example only demonstrates how assertions can be used for checks, but any reasonable program should bail out early in such cases, which would make these assertions redundant, and only add more coupling to upstream, which we're trying to avoid.
+
+```nix
+{ config, lib, ... }: with lib; {
+  # ...
+  config = mkIf cfg.enable {
+    # Examples only for demonstration purposes, don't actually add assertions for such properties
+    assertions = [
+      {
+        assertion = cfg.config.enableLogging or true -> cfg.config ? logLevel;
+        message = "You also need to set `services.foo.config.logLevel` if `services.foo.config.enableLogging` is turned on.";
+      }
+      {
+        assertion = cfg.config ? port -> types.port.check cfg.config.port;
+        message = "${toString cfg.config.port} is not a valid port number for `services.foo.config.port`.";
+      }
+    ];
+  };
+}
+```
+
+TODO: Are there any good examples of using assertions for configuration checks at all?
+
+### Implementation
+
+The implementation consists of three separate parts
+
+#### Configuration types
+
+A set of types for common configuration formats should be provided in `lib.types.config`. Such a type should encode what values can be set in files of this configuration format as a Nix value, with the module system being able to merge multiple values correctly. This is the part that checks whether the user set an encodeable value. This can be extended over time, but could include the following as a start:
+- JSON
+- YAML, which is probably the same as JSON
+- INI
+- A simple `key=value` format
+- A recursive `key.subkey.subsubkey=value` format
